summary: Proposes an experiment in subnetting a class A network address block. The goal was to find and fix software that does not handle subnetted class A addresses. It is an experimental document; results are in RFC 1879.

plainLanguage.summary: This experimental memo reserves class A network 39 for testing how routing software handles subnetted addresses. It describes two temporary ways to assign the remaining address bits.

subtitle: A temporary experiment using IPv4 network 39 to test subnetted class A addresses.

tldr.problem: The memo says some routing software might not handle subnetted class A addresses correctly.
tldr.mechanism: IANA temporarily designated class A network 39 for two address allocation experiments and encouraged routing and name-resolution tests.
tldr.outcome: The planned experiment ran from May 1, 1995 to December 1, 1995. Neither allocation scheme was intended as a future model.

today: RFC 1797 is Experimental. Its text gives December 1, 1995 as the planned termination date, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Test Class A Subnetting
sections.content:
The memo says there was interest in subnetting class A addresses and evidence that some routing software might not handle them correctly. It suggests testing before such addresses became necessary, so software problems could be identified and fixed.

IANA temporarily designated class A network number 39 for the experiment. The RFC says it would begin on May 1, 1995, with a planned termination date of December 1, 1995, and that these addresses could later be reassigned.
sections.plainLanguage: The experiment was meant to find routing software that failed with subnetted class A addresses. Network 39 was set aside for a limited test period.

sections.title: Two Ways to Divide Network 39
sections.content:
The high-order octet is network number 39. In Case 1, the first of the low-order 24 bits is zero, the next 15 bits are the low-order 15 bits of an assigned autonomous system number, and the low-order octet is for local use.

In Case 2, the high-order bit is one and the other 23 bits are assigned by IANA, initially reserved for future use. The intent is to provide prefixes of different lengths. The RFC says neither scheme is a model for future allocation of subnetted class A addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Both schemes start with network number 39. One uses part of an autonomous system number; the other uses a variable prefix assigned by IANA.

sections.title: DNS and Inter-Network Tests
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example in which an address uses network 39, an assigned autonomous system number and a local host value. It says providers are expected to use such addresses for servers supplying popular material through Web or FTP.

DNS name and address resolution should also be provided. The RFC describes A and PTR records and delegation below 39.IN-ADDR.ARPA. It encourages providers to exchange addresses to test portability between allocations, but says that testing is not a model for actual use.
sections.plainLanguage: The experiment also tests whether names resolve to the assigned addresses and whether networks can exchange addresses. The memo says those tests do not define future allocation practice.

sections.title: Security and Experimental Status
sections.content: The memo says security issues are not discussed. It defines an Experimental protocol, not an Internet standard, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvement.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an experiment, not an Internet standard. The memo does not discuss security issues.
